passages.text: In 1993 the American biologists Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun were studying a minuscule worm barely a millimeter long that is widely used in laboratories. They sought to understand why certain mutant worms developed abnormally, with cells following the wrong timetable as the animal grew. Their inquiry led to the discovery of a new kind of molecule: a very short strand of genetic material now called microRNA that carries no instructions for building a protein. Instead, it turns other genes down by latching onto their messages before those messages can be used. At first the finding was dismissed as a curiosity peculiar to worms. Then, in 2000, Ruvkun's team identified a second microRNA that turned out to exist in a vast array of animals, including humans. Researchers now know that the human genome contains more than a thousand microRNAs and that faulty regulation by them is linked to cancer and other diseases. In 2024 the two scientists were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in medicine for this work.

Parchment, made from animal skin, was costly in the Middle Ages, so scribes often scraped earlier writing off a page and used it again. A manuscript produced in this way is called a palimpsest. The most illustrious example is a prayer book assembled in the thirteenth century. Its pages had originally carried a tenth-century copy of works by the Greek mathematician Archimedes, which a scribe washed away, cut apart, and turned sideways before writing prayers on top. The older text survived only as faint vestiges. After the book was sold at auction in 1998, scientists spent years photographing it under different wavelengths of light, which made the erased letters legible again. Among the retrieved works was a treatise known as The Method, of which no other copy survives. It demonstrates Archimedes' reasoning in ways that foreshadow ideas from calculus, developed nearly two thousand years later. A thrifty decision by a medieval scribe thus ended up safeguarding the very text it was meant to remove.

In a classic set of experiments, psychologists gave volunteers pairs of related words to remember. Some participants simply read complete pairs, such as rapid and fast. Others saw the first word together with only the opening letter of the second, and had to supply the rest of it themselves. On a later test, the second group remembered considerably more words, even though their extra effort had lasted only a second or two. Researchers call this the generation effect, and it has been replicated with numbers, definitions, and answers to simple questions. The lesson for students runs against intuition. Rereading a textbook feels productive because the material grows familiar, but familiarity is not the same as memory. A learner who closes the book and tries to reproduce the main ideas from scratch, however haltingly, is more likely to retain them. In short, information that we produce for ourselves, even imperfectly, tends to stay with us longer than information we merely receive.

When the first preserved platypus reached Britain from Australia at the end of the eighteenth century, some naturalists suspected a hoax. The creature seemed to have been assembled from spare parts: a bill like a duck's, a tail like a beaver's, webbed feet, and dense brown fur. One scholar reportedly scrutinized the skin for stitches. Further discoveries only deepened the enigma. The platypus, it turned out, is a mammal that lays eggs, one of only a handful of living species that do so. Males carry venomous spurs on their hind legs, a rarity among mammals. When it hunts underwater, the animal closes its eyes, ears, and nostrils and locates its prey with thousands of receptors in its bill that sense the faint electrical signals produced by the muscles of shrimp and worms. Far from being a jumble of mismatched features, the platypus is now understood as the survivor of an ancient branch of the mammal family, furnishing clues to how the earliest mammals may have lived.

In 1989 the Brazilian city of Porto Alegre tried an experiment that has since been emulated in thousands of cities around the world. Instead of leaving every spending decision to elected officials, it invited inhabitants to neighborhood assemblies where they could debate how part of the city's investment budget should be used and vote on priorities such as paving roads, extending sewers, or building health clinics. Early studies found that more money flowed to poorer districts and that many participants had rarely been involved in politics before. Critics point out that the share of the budget under citizens' control is often small, and that meetings can be dominated by well-organized groups. Those objections deserve scrutiny, but they miss part of the point. The value of such programs lies not only in the projects they fund but also in what participants learn. People who have had to weigh one neighborhood's needs against another's tend to grasp the tradeoffs of government far better than those who merely vote once every few years.

Nearly twenty years after conquering England in 1066, William the Conqueror wanted to know exactly what his new kingdom contained. At Christmas in 1085 he ordered a survey. Over the following year royal commissioners traversed most of the country putting the same set of questions to local juries: who held each piece of land, how many people lived and worked there, how many plows, mills, and animals it had, and what it was worth. The answers were compiled into a manuscript of remarkable detail, the main volume of which seems to have been written by a single scribe. The English came to call it the Domesday Book, likening its verdicts to those of the Last Judgment (Doomsday), against which there could be no appeal. For the king, the survey was a tool for levying taxes and adjudicating disputes over land. For historians, it is something more: a snapshot of an entire society at one moment, recording thousands of villages, many of which still exist. The original is kept at the National Archives in London.

Parents are often told that music lessons will make their children smarter, enhancing not only their musical skill but also their performance in mathematics, reading, and memory. The idea is appealing, and early studies seemed to support it. Children who play instruments do tend to score higher on many tests. Yet such correlations are hard to interpret, since families who pay for music lessons often differ in income, education, and encouragement at home. When researchers have instead randomly assigned children either to music training or to other activities, the picture has become far less compelling. A large analysis that combined dozens of such experiments in 2020 found that once the best-designed studies were considered, the effect of music training on skills outside music was close to zero. None of this means that music lessons are devoid of merit. Learning an instrument brings pleasure, discipline, and a skill that can last a lifetime. Parents may simply be prudent to value music for its own sake rather than as a shortcut to higher grades.

The slime mold Physarum polycephalum is a single cell with no brain or nervous system, yet it can solve problems that would confound many animals. (A) Placed at the entrance of a small maze with food at the exit, it spreads its yellow, branching body through every corridor and then recoils from the dead ends, leaving a single tube along the shortest route. (B) In 2010 a team of Japanese and British researchers took the experiment further. They arranged oat flakes on a damp surface in the positions of cities around Tokyo and let the mold grow among them. (C) Within about a day, it had linked the flakes with a web of tubes strikingly similar to the region's actual railway network, which engineers had refined over many decades. (D) Its method is simple: tubes that carry an abundance of nutrients thicken, while those that carry little gradually wither. Such findings have galvanized computer scientists searching for efficient ways to design networks without any central planner.

In late 2023, regulators in the United Kingdom and then the United States approved a therapy called Casgevy for sickle cell disease, making it the first medicine based on the gene-editing tool CRISPR to reach patients. Sickle cell disease is inherited. A single flaw in the gene for hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells, causes the cells to become stiff and curved. These misshapen cells can obstruct small blood vessels, producing episodes of excruciating pain, organ damage, and a shortened life.
Interestingly, the therapy does not repair the faulty gene itself. Instead, doctors extract a patient's own blood stem cells and edit them to switch back on a form of hemoglobin that the body normally produces only before birth. The edited cells are then returned to the patient, whose remaining bone marrow must first be cleared out with strong chemotherapy. In clinical trials, most patients who received the therapy went at least a year without a single severe pain crisis.
The feat nonetheless raises uncomfortable questions. The process takes months, necessitates specialized hospitals, and carries a price of millions of dollars per patient. Most people with sickle cell disease live in sub-Saharan Africa and India, where such resources are scarce. Unless costs plummet, a cure celebrated as a triumph of science may remain ____ the very patients who need it most.

Many people assume that palliative care begins only when doctors have nothing left to offer, a hushed room where therapy ends and waiting begins. The assumption is understandable but erroneous. Palliative care is specialized medical care aimed at alleviating pain, breathlessness, anxiety, and the other burdens of serious illness, and it can be provided at any stage, alongside therapy intended to cure. Hospice care is a narrower form of it, reserved for people whose illness is expected to end their lives within months and who have chosen to focus on comfort rather than cure.
The distinction matters because the misunderstanding keeps many patients away from help they could use. In a widely cited study published in 2010, patients with advanced lung cancer were randomly assigned either to standard cancer care or to standard care plus early palliative care. Those who met palliative specialists from the start reported a better quality of life and fewer symptoms of depression. They also chose less aggressive therapy near the end of life, yet they unexpectedly lived nearly three months longer on average.
As populations age, demand for this kind of care is escalating faster than the number of trained specialists. Broadening training, and persuading patients that asking for comfort is not the same as giving up, may be among the most humane investments a health system can make.

On April 8, 2024, the Moon passed directly between the Sun and the Earth, casting a shadow that swept across North America from the Pacific coast of Mexico through the United States and into eastern Canada. For those inside the narrow path of totality, the sky darkened for as long as about four and a half minutes, temperatures plunged, and the Sun's faint outer atmosphere known as the corona appeared as a pallid halo. Millions of people flocked to small towns along the path, spawning traffic jams on rural highways, and many communities had spent months preparing with extra portable toilets and emergency staff.
For scientists, the event was also a boon. Because the Moon covers the luminous disk of the Sun almost perfectly, a total eclipse reveals parts of the corona that are hard to study at other times. Researchers launched rockets into the upper atmosphere to gauge how the abrupt darkness affected it, and volunteers across the continent recorded the behavior of animals, many of which acted as if night had fallen.
Total solar eclipses are not rare on a global scale; one occurs somewhere on Earth approximately every year and a half. But any particular place may wait centuries between them, and much of each path crosses open ocean. For most people who watched in 2024, it was probably the only total eclipse they would ever see without traveling far. The next total eclipse visible from the contiguous United States will not come until 2044.

Today the potato is so central to French cooking that it is hard to imagine a time when it was shunned. Yet for much of the eighteenth century, many people in France regarded it with profound suspicion. The plant had come from South America, it belonged to the same family as toxic nightshade, and it was widely believed to cause disease. In some regions it was fed predominantly to livestock; eating it was a mark of abject poverty.
The man most often credited with changing this attitude is Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, a pharmacist in the French army. Captured during the Seven Years' War, he survived months in a Prussian prison largely on potatoes and came home convinced of their worth. After the Paris Faculty of Medicine declared potatoes fit to eat in 1772, he set about winning over the public. He hosted dinners at which every dish was made from potatoes and presented potato flowers to the king and queen. According to a popular story, he also planted a field near Paris and had it guarded by soldiers during the day but <u>left unwatched at night</u>, reasoning that inquisitive neighbors would assume anything so meticulously protected must be valuable.
Whether or not the story is true, it captures something important about Parmentier's approach. The potato's nutritional value had been recognized for years. ____, facts alone had not sufficed to overcome the prejudice against it. What swayed minds was a campaign that altered what the vegetable meant, turning a food of the poor into an object of curiosity, prestige, and even royal favor.

In the early 1990s, two psychologists at Princeton University asked undergraduates two simple questions: how comfortable they personally felt with the heavy drinking prevalent on campus, and how comfortable they thought the average student felt. Most respondents reported considerable unease. Yet they assumed that their classmates were far more nonchalant about drinking than they themselves were. In other words, a substantial number of students inwardly disapproved of a norm that each believed everyone else supported.
Social scientists call this pattern pluralistic ignorance. It arises when people observe one another's public behavior and treat it as a faithful guide to private sentiment, while knowing full well that their own public behavior conceals misgivings. A student who laughs along at a party and accepts another drink concludes that her discomfort is unusual, never suspecting that the laughing classmate beside her is drawing exactly the same conclusion about her.
The pattern helps explain why unpopular customs can endure for long periods. A norm that hardly anyone endorses may persist simply because nobody realizes how few people endorse it. For the same reason, such norms can crumble with startling speed once concealed sentiments become visible, as when an anonymous survey is published or a few individuals voice their misgivings in public. Some universities have tried to harness this insight by sharing accurate survey results with students, on the theory that people who learn what their peers really think will feel ____.

On the first day of 2024, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake convulsed the Noto Peninsula on Japan's western coast, killing hundreds of people and obliterating thousands of wooden houses. Beyond the human toll, the quake wrought a striking geological change. Along parts of the peninsula's northern shore, the land rose by as much as four meters within seconds. Harbors that had sheltered fishing boats for generations were abruptly left high and dry with their floors exposed to the air, and in some places the coastline moved seaward by more than two hundred meters. Geologists explained that the earthquake had occurred on a fault beneath the peninsula, thrusting one block of the crust upward. Comparable uplift has happened there before; flat steps along the coast chronicle earlier episodes over thousands of years. For the fishing communities, however, the change was a practical calamity. Even after roads were repaired and homes rebuilt, boats could not return to ports that no longer reached the sea, and rebuilding the harbors became a protracted and costly undertaking.

The largest extant medieval manuscript in Europe is a book so heavy that it takes two people to lift it. Known as the Codex Gigas, or Giant Book, it was produced in the early thirteenth century, probably at a small Benedictine monastery in Bohemia in what is now the Czech Republic. Its pages are made from the skins of well over a hundred animals and encompass the entire Latin Bible along with a history of Bohemia, medical texts, and a calendar. The book is most renowned, however, for a full-page portrait of the devil, which has earned it the nickname the Devil's Bible. According to legend, a monk who had broken his vows promised to copy the whole book in a single night and called on the devil for help. Scholars who have scrutinized the handwriting reach a less sensational conclusion: the remarkably uniform script suggests that one scribe did the work, but probably over two decades or more. In 1648, near the end of the Thirty Years' War, Swedish troops carried the book off as plunder, and it has remained in Stockholm ever since.

In experiments reported in 1975, two psychologists presented volunteers with a long list of words, one at a time, and asked a quick question about each. Sometimes the question concerned the word's appearance, such as whether it was printed in capital letters. Sometimes it concerned its sound, such as whether it rhymed with another word. And sometimes it concerned its meaning, such as whether it would fit sensibly into a particular sentence. The volunteers were not told that their memory would later be tested. When it was, they recalled far more of the words they had considered for meaning than those they had judged by appearance or sound, even though every word had been displayed for the same length of time. The researchers argued that memory depends less on how long we look at something than on how deeply we think about it. For learners, the lesson is plain: information that is linked to what it actually means is far more likely to stay with us.

Chopping an onion is one of the few kitchen tasks that invariably brings tears to the eyes, and the reason is a small chemical defense system. An intact onion stores sulfur-containing compounds and the enzymes that act on them in separate compartments of its cells. When a knife breaks those cells open, the two come into contact, and a chain of reactions produces a gas that easily drifts into the air. The gas rises to the eyes, where it stimulates nerves that trigger tears to wash the irritant away. In the wild, the same system presumably deters animals from eating the bulb. Several familiar tricks mitigate the effect. Chilling an onion before cutting retards the reactions, a sharp knife damages fewer cells than a dull one, and working near a fan or an open window disperses the gas. A Japanese food company has even reported breeding an onion that produces almost none of the gas, though such varieties are still rare in ordinary shops.

Most laws, once enacted, remain in force until legislators actively repeal them, and repealing a law is usually much harder than passing one. Consequently, legal codes tend to accumulate rules that made sense when they were written but have long outlived their purpose. One remedy is the sunset clause, a provision stating that a law will expire automatically on a set date unless it is renewed. Such clauses have been appended to emergency powers, new taxes, and experimental programs in many countries. Critics lament that they engender uncertainty for businesses and citizens, who cannot be sure whether a rule will endure. Others acknowledge that legislators sometimes renew expiring laws with scant debate, turning the review into a perfunctory ritual. These are genuine weaknesses, yet the underlying idea remains sound. A law that must be justified afresh every few years compels lawmakers to ask whether it is still working, rather than leaving it in place simply because no one has bothered to remove it.

When people bang an elbow on a table, they usually rub the sore spot at once, and the rubbing genuinely seems to help. For much of the early twentieth century, scientists conceived of pain as a simple alarm: damage to the body sent signals along dedicated nerves to the brain, and the strength of the signal determined the strength of the pain. That model struggled to explain everyday observations such as the effect of rubbing, or the way soldiers grievously wounded in battle sometimes reported feeling little pain until they reached safety. In 1965 the psychologist Ronald Melzack and the neuroscientist Patrick Wall proposed what they called the gate control theory. They posited that a kind of gate in the spinal cord regulates how many pain signals pass upward. Signals from touch and pressure, carried by different nerve fibers, can partly close the gate, which is why rubbing soothes the ache. Signals descending from the brain can open or close it as well, depending on attention, fear, and expectation. Although subsequent research has revised many details, the theory altered how doctors understand and treat pain.

Few objects seem as unassuming as the paper clip, yet its history carries a startling load of national pride. In 1899 a Norwegian inventor named Johan Vaaler patented a bent-wire device for holding sheets of paper together, and for much of the twentieth century many Norwegians believed that their countryman had devised the paper clip itself. In fact, Vaaler's design lacked the double loop of the familiar clip. Comparable clips were already being made in Britain, where a version known as the Gem had appeared some years earlier. The legend acquired new significance during the Second World War. While Germany occupied Norway, some Norwegians wore paper clips on their clothing as a quiet sign of resistance and unity, since open protest could lead to arrest. In 1989 a giant paper clip sculpture was erected near Oslo in Vaaler's honor. The story demonstrates how an everyday object can accrue meanings far beyond its function, even when the facts beneath them are shaky.

Ice is slippery, but for more than a century the usual explanation of why was mistaken: it held that the pressure of a skate blade melts a thin film of water beneath it, on which the skater glides. (A) Yet calculations demonstrate that the pressure under an ordinary skate is far too small to melt ice at typical winter temperatures, and people slip on ice even in broad, flat-soled shoes. (B) Another explanation focused on friction: the rubbing of a sliding object might generate enough heat to melt the surface. (C) This effect probably contributes once something is already moving, but it cannot explain why ice is slippery to a person who is standing still. (D) More recent research has shown that the outermost layer of molecules on an ice surface is only loosely bound, even well below freezing, and behaves somewhat like a liquid. These restless molecules act as a lubricant. Scientists still debate the details, but the old pressure explanation, which lingers in some textbooks, has largely been abandoned.

In the 1950s many psychologists believed that infants become attached to their mothers predominantly because mothers provide food. Affection, on this view, was a kind of learned reward. To test this idea, the psychologist Harry Harlow raised infant rhesus monkeys with two artificial mothers: one was made of bare wire but held a bottle of milk, while the other was wrapped in soft cloth but offered no food at all. Yet most of the infants spent nearly all their time clinging to the cloth figure and visited the wire one only briefly to feed, and when something startled them they ran to the cloth mother rather than the one that fed them. The results suggested that comfort and physical contact, not just nourishment, lie at the heart of attachment. The experiments also raised weighty ethical objections, since the young monkeys were deprived of real mothers, and they are now often cited in debates over how laboratory animals should be treated.

When Johann Sebastian Bach died in 1750, he was esteemed chiefly as an organist, and much of his music was regarded as outmoded. Younger composers favored a lighter, simpler style, and for decades his large choral works were rarely performed outside the churches where he had worked. The turning point came in 1829, when the twenty-year-old Felix Mendelssohn conducted the St Matthew Passion in Berlin, its first performance since Bach's death. The concert caused a sensation and kindled a revival that eventually led to the publication of Bach's complete works and cemented his place among the greatest composers. Within a few decades, scholars had begun collecting and editing manuscripts that had lain scattered among his heirs and former pupils. The story is a reminder that reputations are not fixed at the moment of an artist's death; they are shaped, and sometimes rescued, by later generations who decide what is worth remembering.

Artificial intelligence now reads medical images in hospitals around the world. Software trained on millions of scans can flag a suspicious shadow on a chest X-ray or a minuscule lesion on a mammogram. In some studies, such tools have matched or exceeded the accuracy of experienced radiologists on narrowly defined tasks. Regulators in several countries have cleared hundreds of these products for clinical use.
Their proliferation has raised a question that the law has not yet answered clearly: when an AI-assisted diagnosis goes wrong, who is accountable? Conventionally, a physician who misreads a scan may be held liable for negligence. But if a radiologist follows an AI tool's advice and the advice proves wrong, part of the blame might seem to belong to the company that built it. Conversely, a doctor who overrides a correct AI warning may face hard questions about why the machine was ignored. Some legal scholars fret that this uncertainty pushes doctors toward defensive behavior, either deferring to the software to protect themselves or refusing to use it at all.
Most experts agree that more explicit rules are needed. Proposals include mandating that manufacturers share data on how their tools perform across different groups of patients, recording when and why doctors accept or reject AI suggestions, and creating insurance schemes that spread the risk. Without such measures, a technology meant to make diagnosis safer could leave both patients and physicians in legal limbo.

In many affluent countries, the number of people who need help with everyday tasks such as bathing, dressing, and eating is growing quickly as populations age. The number of people willing to provide that help is not. Care work is physically taxing and emotionally grueling, and it is often poorly paid, so many workers leave within a few years. Families, conventionally the main source of care, are smaller than they once were, and adult children frequently live far from their parents or hold full-time jobs.
Governments have responded in several ways. Some have boosted wages in publicly funded care homes or offered training subsidies. Others have turned to migration: Japan has created visa categories that allow workers from countries such as Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines to work in nursing care, while care homes in much of Europe rely heavily on staff born abroad. Technology offers further avenues, from sensors that detect falls to machines that help lift patients from their beds, though such devices cannot provide the conversation and companionship that many older people value most.
____, none of these responses alone is likely to close the gap. Experts increasingly argue that the problem is not simply a dearth of hands but a failure to value care. As long as looking after others is treated as unskilled work, they warn, it will be difficult to attract enough people to do it.

In parts of sub-Saharan Africa, a small brown bird called the greater honeyguide has formed an unusual partnership with people. The bird feeds on beeswax, but it cannot easily break into the nests of wild bees, which are often concealed inside trees and defended by thousands of stinging insects. Human honey hunters, for their part, can open the nests with axes and calm the bees with smoke, but they cannot easily find them. So the two collaborate. The bird attracts a hunter's attention with a chattering call and flies ahead from tree to tree, leading the way to a nest. After the hunters have taken the honey, the bird eats the wax left behind.
In 2016 researchers working with Yao honey hunters in Mozambique demonstrated that the communication runs in both directions. The hunters use a special trilling sound to summon honeyguides, and in experiments, playing a recording of this call more than doubled the chance of being guided to a nest compared with recordings of other sounds. Subsequent research found that hunters in Tanzania use a different call, a melodious whistle, and that birds in each region respond most strongly to their local signal. The relationship, in other words, appears to be ____, passed down among both the people and the birds of each area.

Florence Nightingale is remembered as the lamp-carrying nurse who tended wounded British soldiers during the Crimean War in the 1850s. Less widely known is that she was also a pioneering statistician. At the military hospital in Scutari near Constantinople, she found overcrowded wards, poor drainage, and contaminated water, and she began keeping meticulous records of how soldiers died. Her figures demonstrated that far more men were dying from diseases such as cholera and typhus, spread by filthy conditions, than from wounds received in battle.
Back in Britain, Nightingale confronted the challenge of persuading officials and politicians who had scant patience for tables of numbers. She therefore presented her data in a form that anyone could grasp at a glance: a circular diagram divided into wedges, one for each month, with areas shaded to show deaths from different causes. The vast wedges representing preventable disease made the scale of the problem impossible to ignore. Her diagrams helped induce the government to overhaul sanitation in military hospitals and barracks, and in 1858 she became the first woman elected to the Royal Statistical Society.
Nightingale's example remains instructive today. Collecting accurate data is only the first step; changing policy necessitates presenting that data in a way that ____.

In the 1970s the Bangladeshi economist Muhammad Yunus began lending small sums of money to poor villagers, most of them women, who had no access to conventional banks. Borrowers were organized into small groups whose members were accountable for one another's repayments, an arrangement that lessened the need for collateral. Repayment rates were strikingly high, and the Grameen Bank, which grew out of this work, became a model copied around the world. In 2006 Yunus and the bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize, and microfinance was widely hailed as a potent weapon against poverty.
Subsequent research painted a more modest picture. In 2015 a group of economists published the results of six randomized studies carried out in countries on four continents. Access to small loans did help some households start or expand businesses and gave them more flexibility in managing their money. Yet the studies found no consistent evidence that microcredit revolutionized the lives of typical borrowers by substantially raising their incomes or enhancing their health and schooling.
These findings do not mean that microfinance has failed. Reliable access to credit and savings is valuable to poor households, as it is to everyone else. What they suggest is that no single financial product is likely to end poverty, and that grandiose claims about tools for development should be tested before they are widely acclaimed.

When Hurricane Helene made landfall on the Gulf Coast of Florida in late September 2024, much of the scrutiny focused on the shoreline. The worst destruction, however, came hundreds of kilometers inland in the mountains of western North Carolina, a region that many inhabitants had regarded as a haven from climate calamities. Days of torrential rain before the storm had already saturated the ground, and Helene's remnants then unleashed record amounts of water on steep slopes. Rivers rose with harrowing speed, landslides ravaged roads and houses, and towns in narrow valleys were marooned for days without power, water, or telephone service. More than two hundred people died across several states, many of them far from the coast. Few households in the mountains had flood insurance, since the risk had seemed negligible. The disaster raised disquieting questions about how flood risk is mapped, and about whether any place can be deemed safe as warmer air holds more moisture and storms carry heavier rain farther from the sea.

Among the oldest customer complaints known is a clay tablet written about 3,750 years ago in the city of Ur, in what is now southern Iraq. Its author is a man named Nanni. He addresses a merchant called Ea-nasir, who had agreed to supply him with copper ingots. Nanni's indignation is evident even in translation. The copper he received, he writes, was of shoddy quality, and his messengers had been treated with contempt and sent back empty-handed. He demands a full refund and declares that he will no longer accept inferior metal. The tablet now resides in the British Museum, and in recent years it has become something of an online sensation, shared as ostensible proof that bad customer service is nothing new. For historians, its significance lies elsewhere. Together with other complaint letters unearthed in the same house, it demonstrates that long-distance trade in the ancient Near East relied on credit, written agreements, and reputations that a single vitriolic letter could damage.

In one experiment, office workers were asked to choose a snack that they would receive a week later: either a piece of fruit or a less healthy treat such as a chocolate bar. Some made the choice late in the afternoon, when they were likely to be hungry; others chose just after lunch. Those who chose while hungry were considerably more likely to pick the unhealthy snack, even though they would not eat it until the following week, when their hunger at that moment would no longer matter. Economists call this tendency projection bias: people assume that their future preferences will resemble their present ones. It helps explain why shoppers who visit a supermarket on an empty stomach cram their carts with food they later regret, and why people who sign gym contracts in a burst of January zeal often stop going within weeks. In each case, a transient state of mind is mistaken for a lasting feature of who we are.

The superb lyrebird of southeastern Australia is named for the male's spectacular tail, which he fans over his head during courtship displays. Yet the bird is even more remarkable for its voice. Besides its own calls, a male lyrebird weaves into his song uncanny imitations of dozens of other species from kookaburras to whipbirds. Young birds appear to learn many of these imitations from older lyrebirds rather than directly from the species they copy. Recordings made near human settlements have also captured lyrebirds reproducing the clicks of camera shutters, car alarms, and chainsaws, although such feats are rarer than popular videos suggest. Research published in 2021 unveiled something more startling still. During mating, males sometimes produce a chaotic medley resembling a whole flock of birds raising the alarm about a predator, perhaps to induce the female to stay close. The lyrebird's song, in other words, is not merely a collection of copies but a performance with purposes of its own.

For generations, public libraries levied small fines for overdue books, on the assumption that the threat of a sanction would spur borrowers to return items on time. In recent years, however, many libraries in the United States and elsewhere have abolished such fines altogether. Their rationale is partly pragmatic. Fines brought in comparatively little money, and collecting them consumed staff time. More importantly, librarians noticed that the people most likely to have their cards blocked over unpaid fines were children and low-income families, precisely the people libraries most wanted to serve. When large city systems such as Chicago's dropped their fines, they reported that many long-missing books resurfaced and that lapsed borrowers returned as well. Libraries still expect materials to be returned, and most continue to charge for lost items. But the experience suggests that a sanction designed to safeguard a shared resource can end up keeping people away from it. A rule deserves to be judged by what it actually achieves, not only by what it was meant to do.

Peter Mark Roget was an esteemed London physician and scientist, but he is remembered today for a book that began as a private pastime. As a young man in the early 1800s, Roget started compiling lists of words grouped by their meanings, partly as a way of soothing an apprehensive mind. Several members of his family suffered from depression, and the methodical work of classification seems to have steadied him. For decades the lists remained a personal tool for pinpointing the apt expression. Only after retiring did he expand them into a book, published in 1852 as the Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases, a title drawn from a Greek word for a treasure house. Unlike a dictionary, which leads from a word to its meaning, the thesaurus leads from an idea to the words that might express it. It was an instant success and has never gone out of print. Roget kept revising it until his death at ninety, and later editions were prepared by his son and grandson.

Reading picture books aloud to young children is widely advocated, but researchers at Ohio State University set out to gauge just how much language such reading provides. In a study published in 2019, they counted the words in the books most often borrowed from libraries for children under five and calculated how many words a child would hear under different reading habits. The results were striking. A child read five books a day from birth would hear approximately 1.4 million more words by the age of five than a child who was never read to. Even a single book a day added up to nearly three hundred thousand words. The researchers pointed out that books contain vocabulary rarely heard in everyday conversation at home, such as the names of unusual animals or descriptions of faraway places, which may help explain why children who are read to tend to start school with larger vocabularies. The figures are estimates rather than measurements of any particular child, but they demonstrate how small daily habits can accumulate into large differences.

Noise-canceling headphones seem almost miraculous: switch them on, and the roar of an airplane engine dwindles to a faint hum. Yet the principle behind them is elementary physics. Sound travels as a wave of minuscule pressure changes in the air, and two waves that meet can add together or cancel each other out. (A) A small microphone on the outside of each ear cup continuously picks up the surrounding noise. (B) A chip then generates a second sound wave that is the mirror image of the first, with its peaks lined up against the original wave's troughs. (C) When the two waves meet inside the ear cup, they largely cancel, and the listener hears much less of the noise. (D) The technique works best on steady, low-pitched sounds such as the drone of engines, which change little from moment to moment and are therefore easy to predict. Abrupt or high-pitched noises, such as voices or a baby's cry, are harder to cancel, which is why the headphones also rely on padding that physically blocks sound.

On September 7, 2025, in a ceremony in St. Peter's Square, Pope Leo XIV proclaimed Carlo Acutis a saint, making him the first member of the millennial generation to be canonized by the Catholic Church. Acutis, born in 1991 and raised in Milan, died of leukemia in 2006 at the age of fifteen. In many ways he was an ordinary teenager of his time: he played video games, relished football, and was fascinated by computers. He taught himself programming and built a website chronicling reported Eucharistic miracles around the world, which later became the basis for exhibitions in many countries. Friends and teachers also remembered his benevolence toward classmates who were bullied and toward homeless people in his neighborhood.
His canonization had originally been scheduled for April 2025 but was deferred after the death of Pope Francis. When the ceremony finally took place, it drew a large throng of young pilgrims, many of whom saw in Acutis a paragon of faith lived out in a digital world rather than in spite of it.
Church officials have portrayed his life as a message about technology. The internet, in this view, is neither good nor evil in itself; what matters is the purpose for which it is used. For a generation that spends much of its life online, the example of a teenage saint who used his screen to serve others has manifest appeal.

Smartphone apps that promise to alleviate anxiety, buoy mood, or improve sleep have proliferated in recent years, and millions of people have downloaded them. Their allure is easy to grasp. In many countries, waiting lists for therapy stretch for months, and some people balk at seeking help in person because of cost or embarrassment. An app is available at any hour, often for free, and it can be used in private.
The evidence, however, is patchy. Some apps are built on established methods such as cognitive behavioral therapy, and a number of controlled studies have found modest benefits, particularly for mild symptoms. ____, many others have never been tested at all. Reviews of popular apps have also found that a large share of users abandon them within a few weeks, which curtails whatever good they might do. Privacy is another concern. Some apps have been caught sharing sensitive information with advertisers, and users rarely read the policies that explain what happens to their data.
None of this means that such apps are futile. For some people they may serve as a first step, a way to learn rudimentary coping skills or to recognize that further help is needed. The peril lies in treating them as a substitute for professional care when symptoms are serious, or in assuming that an app marketed as healthy has been shown to work.

Beavers once lived along rivers throughout Britain, but they were hunted to extinction there by around the sixteenth century, prized for their fur and for a substance from their glands used in medicine and perfume. Their return has been incremental and, at times, unofficial. A licensed trial began in Scotland in 2009, while in England beavers of dubious origin, probably escaped or illicitly released animals, settled on several rivers. In 2022 beavers became a legally protected species in England, and in early 2025 the government approved licensed releases of beavers into the wild.
Proponents argue that beavers are adept engineers whose work benefits whole landscapes. Their dams impede the flow of water, creating ponds and wetlands that shelter insects, fish, and birds, store water during droughts, and can reduce the peak of floods downstream. Studies of beaver sites in England have found that water flowing out of them is often cleaner than water flowing in.
Not everyone is enthusiastic. Some farmers fret that dams will inundate valuable fields or that beavers will fell trees in orchards and woodland. Wildlife agencies have devised management plans that allow troublesome dams to be dismantled or lowered. The beaver's return, then, is likely to be a negotiation rather than a simple homecoming: the animals can reshape a landscape for the better, but only if people are willing to ____.

For much of the twentieth century, charitable giving in many countries followed a familiar pattern. Donors wrote checks to large established organizations, often once a year, and trusted those organizations to decide how the money should be spent. In recent decades that pattern has been changing. Online platforms now allow people to give small amounts instantly, to individuals as well as institutions, and crowdfunding sites host campaigns for everything from disaster relief to a neighbor's medical bills. Many younger donors in particular prefer monthly contributions to a single annual gift, and they increasingly expect to see evidence of what their money has achieved.
These changes have manifest merits. Giving has become easier, and people in dire need can sometimes raise money within hours. Yet researchers have noted drawbacks as well. Campaigns that thrive online tend to be those with poignant stories, striking photographs, and well-connected organizers, so help may flow less to the neediest than to the most visible. Crowdfunding for medical costs, in particular, can reward people who are adept at promoting themselves while others with equally serious needs receive little. Studies in several countries have also found that while the total amount donated has held up, the share of households that give anything at all has declined.
Some charities have responded by underscoring transparency and by inviting donors into longer relationships rather than one-time transactions. The challenge is to retain the speed and personal connection of the new forms of giving without letting generosity depend on ____.

When William Shakespeare died in 1616, about half of his plays had never been printed. Those that had appeared in print were published in cheap single editions known as quartos, some meticulously prepared, others apparently pieced together from actors' memories and full of garbled lines. Plays were regarded as working scripts belonging to an acting company, not as literature worth preserving, and many works by Shakespeare's contemporaries have been lost entirely.
Seven years after his death, his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell compiled thirty-six of his plays into a single large volume, now known as the First Folio. In their preface, they claimed to offer the plays as Shakespeare had written them, disparaging some earlier editions as <u>stolen and deceptive copies</u>. Their claims cannot be taken entirely at face value, since they also had a vested interest in selling the book. Still, the volume preserved eighteen plays that had never been printed before, including Macbeth, The Tempest, Twelfth Night, and Julius Caesar. Without it, these works might well have vanished.
Around 750 copies are thought to have been printed, of which approximately 235 survive. They are among the most coveted printed books in the world, and a copy sold at auction in 2020 for nearly ten million dollars. Yet their true worth lies in what two actors chose to salvage at a time when few people believed plays deserved salvaging.
